newsitem.title: GERMANY: German employer group demands union curbs.
newsitem.headline: German employer group demands union curbs.

text.p: Gesamtmetall, one of Germany's largest employers' federations, called on Monday for new laws that would curb the power of trade unions after it suffered a major setback in regional talks over sick pay last week.
Werner Stumpfe, head of the federation of German metal and engineering employers, said the laws should make industrial action including all-out strikes by workers more difficult.
"We need alternatives so that strikes, as a means of industrial action that damages companies and jobs, are no longer required," Stumpfe said on German radio.
Gesamtmetall said on Sunday resistance by metal and engineering workers had made a new law cutting sick pay costs unenforceable in the sector.

His comments came as employers in the banking industry -- which had been virtually alone among employers in enforcing the law -- also agreed to postpone making the cuts until a wider wage deal wih trade unions had been agreed.
German industrial relations have plummeted to new lows since the introduction of the law in October, cutting sick payments from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.

In reference to a dispute that has included walk-outs by hundreds of thousands of German engineering workers over the past two months, Stumpfe said labour law needed to be changed "so that we don't have to fight each other like Neandertals".
Under clauses in metal and engineering wage contracts, workers are not allowed to strike until after a four-week "cooling off" period following the termination of existing contracts.

This has not however stopped them downing tools for up to a day at a time in protests that have cost firms such as Daimler-Benz AG's Mercedes car-making unit tens of millions of marks in lost production.

With the IG Metall union -- the world's largest trade union with nearly three million members -- warning of all-out strikes next year, employers in the sector have now started to back down on implementing the sick pay law.
Gesamtmetall acknowledged on Sunday it would have to live with a regional wage deal signed in the sector last week that did not implement the sick pay law.
Stumpfe said that although the deal in the northern state of Lower Saxony was "very disappointing", it accepted that it would likely set the tone for settlements in other regions.

Other wage pacts maintaining full sick pay are now seen as likely for metal and engineering workers in much larger states including the steel-making region of North Rhine-Westphalia, where nearly a million people are employed in the sector.
Stumpfe's demand for curbs to union power was later attacked by union officials as aggravating already dire industrial relations throughout the country.
"It's like trying to put out a fire with petrol," Dieter Schulte, chairman of the German Federation of Trade Unions (DGB) said in a statement.
Bank workers managed to extract the climb-down from their employers despite launching the unannounced strikes that they say their contracts allow them to pursue.

But workers in industries such as the much smaller confectionery sector, where there is also no mandatory cooling-off period, have already notched up a series of successes after their two-week strike.
The German unit of Swiss food giant Nestle SA on Sunday became the latest producer in the sector to back down on the sick pay cuts after strikes at its Hamburg and Berlin plants.
